claims.text: As-fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure.
The HfNbTiVAl10 heterostructure includes nanoscale phases or precipitates embedded in a matrix.
A surrogate model can be trained using experimentally quantified microstructural descriptors and initial mechanical-test data.
High-resolution imaging or atom-probe tomography can rapidly extract the key heterostructural metrics needed by the model.
The distribution and volume fraction of nanoscale phases and precipitates link the alloy's microstructure to its macroscopic mechanical response.
The nanoscale features govern local stress distributions during deformation.
The nanoscale features affect defect dynamics through mechanisms such as dislocation pinning.
The nanoscale features influence fracture through crack-path deflection.
Integrating the quantified microstructural features into the ML model captures essential physics governing elastic and fracture behavior.
The surrogate approach bypasses time-consuming atomistic simulations.

Explicit evaluation of fracture or yield strength is largely out of reach for available DFT implementations and first-principles simulations of disordered multi-principal-element alloys remain challenging.
The ML surrogate will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture response more accurately than conventional DFT or MD approaches.
The ML surrogate will predict the target properties faster than conventional simulation methods.
The surrogate may fail when the tested microstructure lies outside the parameter space represented in its training data.
Unexpected local defects or phase distributions may dominate the mechanical response and cause model failure.
The surrogate may fail at strain rates or temperatures not represented in its training data.
Independent tensile and fracture measurements can be used to test predictions of Young's modulus, 0.2% offset yield strength, and fracture response.
The hypothesis is falsified if surrogate prediction errors exceed its established uncertainty range or the errors of conventional simulations.
